title: Cannabis Trichomes 101: What They Are and Why They Matter
h1: Trichomes Explained: The Tiny Glands Behind Potency and Aroma
metaDescription: What cannabis trichomes are, the three main types, how they make cannabinoids and terpenes, what their color means at harvest and how they become kief and hash.
excerpt: Trichomes are the tiny resin glands that make a flower's cannabinoids and terpenes. Here's how they work, what growers watch for at harvest and what frost can and can't tell you.
keyTakeaways: Trichomes are tiny resin glands, concentrated on the flowers of female plants, that make and store cannabinoids such as THCA along with terpenes.
Of the three glandular types, the big stalked trichomes produce the most cannabinoids and most of the visible frost.
Trichome heads turn from clear to milky to amber or brown as flowers mature. Growers use the shift to time harvest, but it is an estimate.
A frosty look isn't proof of potency: research finds trichome density alone doesn't reliably predict cannabinoid content.
Kief, hash and most extracts are collected trichomes, and rough handling, heat and light wear them down.
body:
Cannabis trichomes are the microscopic resin glands behind the frosty, sugar-dusted look of well-grown flower. They aren't decoration. Trichomes are where the plant makes and stores its cannabinoids, including THCA, along with most of the terpenes behind its aroma. Here's what they are, the main types, how growers read them at harvest and how they become kief and hash.

## What cannabis trichomes are and why plants make them

What are trichomes, exactly? A trichome is a small outgrowth on a plant's surface. In cannabis, the ones that matter most are glandular trichomes, which produce resin. On a female plant, the stalked glandular trichomes cluster on the calyxes and bracts of the flowers and spill onto the sugar leaves around them. Male plants make only small amounts of cannabinoids, so growers focus on female flowers. Our [plant anatomy guide](/blog/anatomy-of-cannabis-plant-from-seed-to-bud/) shows where those parts are.

Why does the plant bother? The clues point to defense: THC may help shield the plant from ultraviolet light, and some terpenes repel insects. Sealing these compounds inside a gland also protects the plant, since THCA can be toxic to plant cells.

## Types of trichomes: bulbous, sessile and stalked

Scientists sorted the glandular trichomes on cannabis flowers into three types in the 1970s, using an electron microscope. They differ mostly in size and in whether the head sits on a stalk.

| Type | Shape | What to know |
|---|---|---|
| Bulbous | Tiny and low to the surface | The smallest of the three |
| Capitate-sessile | A round head on a very short stalk | Most common early in flowering |
| Capitate-stalked | A larger head on a long stalk | Produces the most cannabinoids and most of the visible frost |

In a microscope study of two high-THC strains, glandular heads measured 40 to 110 micrometers across, and stalks ranged from 20 to 1,100 micrometers long. Other researchers found that capitate-stalked trichomes appear to grow from sessile-looking ones as the flower matures.

## Inside the gland: how trichomes make cannabinoids and terpenes

Each glandular head works like a tiny factory. Secretory disc cells at its base build cannabinoids, terpenes and flavonoids, and the finished compounds collect in a cavity just under the head's outer skin.

The plant makes cannabinoids in acid form, so fresh flower holds mostly THCA and CBDA rather than THC and CBD. Heat converts the acids, which is why smoking, vaping and baking activate THC. Slower conversion also happens in storage, and its pace depends mainly on temperature and light.

Chemistry shifts with maturity, too: stalked trichomes lean toward lighter, more volatile terpenes called monoterpenes, while sessile ones carry a different mix.

## Trichome color at harvest: clear, cloudy, amber

Under a jeweler's loupe, trichome heads change color as the flower ripens. The resin cavity starts out clear, turns milky white and can end up amber to dark brown as the head ages. Many growers use that shift to time the harvest:

- **Clear:** the flower is still developing.
- **Cloudy or milky:** many growers aim to harvest in this window.
- **Amber:** heads are aging, and some growers wait for a share of amber before they cut.

This is a grower's habit, not settled science. Trichomes on one bud don't all mature at once, and strain and plant age change the pace, so a color check is an estimate. You'll also hear that amber trichomes make for a more sedating high. Some THC does break down into CBN as cannabis ages, but the idea that amber heads change the high is grower lore, not a proven effect.

## Collecting trichomes: dry sift, ice-water hash, kief and extraction

Nearly every concentrate starts by separating trichomes from the plant.

- **Kief.** Loose trichome heads that shake off dried flower and collect under a grinder's screen. Our guide to [what kief is](/blog/what-is-kief/) covers how people use it.
- **Dry sift.** Dried flower is rubbed or tumbled over a series of fine screens that sort the heads by size. The cleanest grades are mostly trichome heads, with little plant material.
- **Ice-water hash.** Buds or trim get agitated in icy water, which makes the heads brittle enough to snap off. The resin is filtered through mesh bags and dried, and pressing it with gentle heat makes rosin.
- **Solvent extraction.** Butane, propane, ethanol or CO2 dissolves the resin, and the solvent is then removed. Our overview of [types of cannabis extraction](/blog/types-of-cannabis-extraction/) explains each method.

Some makers freeze plants right after harvest to keep more of the fresh terpenes, the idea behind the products we compare in [live resin vs. live rosin](/blog/live-resin-vs-live-rosin/).

## Trichomes and potency: what frost means when you shop

**Frost isn't proof of potency.** A heavy coat of trichomes looks impressive, and many shoppers read it as strength. A 2025 review found that trichome density alone doesn't reliably predict cannabinoid content, because trichome shape, size and maturity matter too. The lab-tested numbers tell you more, and a Michigan label shows the THC and CBD content plus the harvest date.

**Handle buds gently.** Trichome heads are fragile. Rough handling and drying change their shape, and every squeeze knocks some resin loose.

**Store flower to protect the resin.** Heat and light speed up the chemical changes inside trichomes. Keep flower sealed airtight and stored in a cool, dark spot. Our guide on [how to store cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) has the details.

The products in our stores come from trusted vendors and have passed Michigan's required testing. [Browse flower on your store's menu](/shop/) to compare lab-tested THC, or ask our budtenders to help in person. Recreational shopping is available to adults 21 and older. Enjoy cannabis responsibly.

faq.a: They make and store the compounds people value in cannabis. Glandular trichomes produce cannabinoids such as THCA, plus terpenes and flavonoids, and hold them in a resin-filled head. For the plant, they likely serve as defense: THC may help block ultraviolet light, and some terpenes repel insects. For you, they're the source of a flower's potency and aroma.

faq.q: Does more frost mean stronger cannabis?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Frost tells you there are plenty of trichomes, but research finds that trichome density alone doesn't reliably predict how much THC a flower contains. Trichome size, maturity and genetics all play a part. To compare strength, check the lab-tested THC printed on each label rather than judging by looks.

faq.q: What color should trichomes be at harvest?
faq.a: Many growers harvest when most trichome heads look cloudy or milky, often with a small share turning amber. Clear heads suggest the flower is still developing. Think of it as a practical guide rather than a precise test, since trichomes on one bud mature at different times.

Yes. Kief is a collection of loose trichome heads that have shaken off dried flower, often gathered in the bottom chamber of a grinder. Because it's mostly resin glands, kief is usually stronger than the flower it came from. It's also the starting point for traditional pressed hash.

claims.claim: Trichomes are where the plant makes and stores its cannabinoids (including THCA) and most of the terpenes behind a flower's aroma.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ (Tanney 2021: metabolites incl. cannabinoids and terpenes formed in secretory disk cells, stored in the subcuticular cavity); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ (Alberti 2025: stalked capitate trichomes 'often regarded as the principal source of cannabinoids and terpenes within female inflorescences')

claims.claim: Stalked glandular trichomes cluster on calyxes and bracts and extend onto sugar leaves.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('primarily concentrated on the calyces and bracts ... with populations extending to the inflorescence sugar leaves')

claims.claim: Male plants make only small amounts of cannabinoids, so growers focus on female flowers.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('While male plants produce small amounts of cannabinoids ... the primary products are the female flowers')

claims.claim: Defense role: THC may help shield the plant from UV light and some terpenes repel insects.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ (hypothesis that THC protects against UV; alpha-pinene and limonene repel insects); stated as hypotheses in the article

claims.claim: THCA can be toxic to plant cells, so storing it inside the gland protects the plant.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('Secreted compounds, including THCA, can be toxic to plant cells; therefore, metabolite storage in the cavity ... affords protection')

claims.claim: Scientists sorted cannabis flower glandular trichomes into three types in the 1970s using an electron microscope.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ (three types described by scanning electron microscopy, Hammond and Mahlberg 1973)

claims.claim: Bulbous are the smallest and low; capitate-sessile have a round head on a very short stalk; capitate-stalked have a larger head on a long stalk and produce the most cannabinoids.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('of the three trichome types, stalked trichomes produce the greatest amount of cannabinoids'); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ ('Bulbous trichomes are the smallest')

claims.claim: Capitate-stalked trichomes make most of the visible frost.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ (stalked capitate trichomes 'are most visible to the naked eye during the later flowering stages, creating the characteristic frosty appearance')

claims.claim: Capitate-sessile trichomes are most common early in flowering.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('sessile-capitate trichomes predominated at 3 weeks')

claims.claim: In a study of two high-THC strains, glandular heads measured 40-110 micrometers and stalks 20-1,100 micrometers.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('Glandular heads ranged from 40 to 110 um in diameter'; stalk length 'from 20 to 1100 um'; genotypes Moby Dick and Space Queen, high-THC)

claims.claim: Capitate-stalked trichomes appear to develop from sessile-looking ones.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31469934/ (Livingston 2020 abstract via Europe PMC: 'stalked trichomes develop from apparently sessile trichomes')

claims.claim: Secretory disc cells at the head's base make cannabinoids, terpenes and flavonoids, stored in a cavity under the head's outer skin.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('Metabolites, including cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids, are formed within secretory disk cells ... and stored in the subcuticular cavity')

claims.claim: Fresh flower holds mostly THCA and CBDA; heat converts them; conversion in storage depends mainly on temperature and light.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('Fresh cannabis flower tissue contains relatively low levels of THC and CBD and higher levels of THCA and CBDA ... the rate of conversion is primarily dependent on temperature and light')

claims.claim: Stalked trichomes lean toward monoterpenes; sessile ones carry a different mix.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31469934/ (stalked: 'strongly monoterpene-dominant'; sessile: 'less monoterpene-dominant')

claims.claim: Trichome heads go from clear to milky white to amber or dark brown as they age.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('transitions from clear (translucent) to cloudy (milky white) and progresses to amber (brown)'); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ ('clear subcuticular cavity ... will turn milky white to dark brown')

claims.claim: Harvest timing by trichome color is grower practice and only an estimate, since trichomes on one bud mature at different times.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('asynchronous development and maturation of stalked-capitate trichomes could present a challenge in achieving a consistent predicted measure of maturation')

claims.claim: Some THC breaks down into CBN as cannabis ages; 'amber means a sedating high' is lore.
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41698831/ (abstract: 'Cannabinol, an oxidative by-product of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol'); the sedation idea is stated as unproven, per the brief

claims.claim: Dry sift: 'The finest grades carry the least plant material.'
claims.fix: Ambiguous: the smallest (finest) sieve fractions carry more plant dust, not less. Reworded to 'The cleanest grades are mostly trichome heads, with little plant material.'
claims.source: general knowledge of sieve grading (low-risk; no figure stated)

claims.claim: Kief, ice-water hash, rosin and solvent (butane, propane, ethanol, CO2) extraction descriptions; fresh-frozen plants for live products.
claims.source: general knowledge; no figures or health claims

claims.claim: A 2025 review found trichome density alone doesn't reliably predict cannabinoid content 'because head size, maturity and genetics matter too'.
claims.fix: The review names trichome shape, size, maturity and surface changes under stress, not genetics. Reworded to 'because trichome shape, size and maturity matter too'.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ ('trichome density alone is unlikely to be directly correlated with cannabinoid content, as trichome shape, size, maturity, and vegetal surface expansion/shrinkage during stress also play a significant role'); article-type review-article

claims.claim: Shoppers often read frost as a sign of potency.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ ('often perceived by consumers as an indicator of higher potency and quality')

claims.claim: FAQ: trichome size, maturity and genetics all play a part in how much THC a flower holds.
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12300688/ (size, maturity); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('variability in developmental stage and maturation between genotypes can potentially lead to variation in total cannabinoid levels')

claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071647/ ('Post-harvest handling and drying were shown to affect trichome morphology')

review.notes: Independent fact-check 2026-10-24 (batch 9). Sources opened as full text through Europe PMC (PMC8488169, PMC10071647, PMC12300688) and the Europe PMC abstract record (PMID 31469934, 41698831). All five listed sources exist, are https and support the sentences they back. Three fixes: the 2025 review's reasons (genetics removed from its attribution), an ambiguous dry-sift grade sentence, and an overstated 'every product' line about High Society.
review.writerNotes: Low-risk article, re-read and revised 2026-10-24: head and stalk sizes now attributed as the study states (glandular heads, not stalked heads), the amber/CBN sentence clarified, the closing vendor sentence reworded away from the About page wording. Harvest color framed as grower practice and amber couch-lock as lore (brief mustAvoid). THC-to-CBN breakdown with age, kief, dry sift, ice-water hash and solvent extraction are general knowledge. No stock claims; the /shop/ link sits only in the closing shopping paragraph.
